findings.title: Denial-cache key can collide across distinct (name, parentFolder) pairs
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey builds the cache key by naively concatenating userUID, action, name and parent with '_' as separator: namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. Because resource UIDs (name/parentFolder) can themselves legally contain underscores, two different requests can produce the same concatenated string, e.g. name="ab_cd", parent="ef" and name="ab", parent="cd_ef" both yield "..._ab_cd_ef". When this happens, a denial cached for one (name, parent) pair will be served for an unrelated resource, causing an incorrect 'denied' result to be returned for a resource the caller actually has access to (or, if the collision is reversed, the opposite type of mistake could occur with other callers sharing the key space). This is a correctness/security risk introduced by the new denial cache, since the previous caches never combined multiple variable-length, potentially-overlapping fields into one key this way.

findings.title: permDenialCache keyed on raw subject UID instead of canonical resolved UID
findings.body: The denial-cache key uses checkReq.UserUID directly (the raw identifier parsed from the Subject string), whereas every other cache in this service (idCache, permCache, teamCache, basicRoleCache) is keyed on the canonical identifier returned by GetUserIdentifiers (userIdentifiers.UID), which can resolve either a numeric ID or a UID to the same canonical value. If different callers pass the subject using different formats (numeric internal ID vs. UID) for the same user, the denial cache will never be shared between them, defeating the purpose of the cache and creating inconsistent caching behavior between the positive permission cache and the new denial cache.

findings.title: New denial cache can reintroduce the staleness problem this PR is meant to fix
findings.body: After a Check() call determines (via a fresh DB query) that a user is not allowed to access a resource, the result is cached for shortCacheTTL (30s) via permDenialCache.Set. If the user is subsequently granted access to that exact resource (e.g., permission is shared, or role changed) within that 30s window, Check() will short-circuit on the denial cache (lines 117-121) and return Allowed=false without consulting the DB, even though the user now has permission. This is the same category of staleness bug the PR is trying to fix for newly-created resources (stale positive cache), but now reintroduced via the new negative cache for recently-denied lookups.

findings.title: Permission-cache usage metric mislabeled when cache is hit but check is denied
findings.body: In Check(), when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cache hit but checkPermission on the cached permissions evaluates to false, execution falls through past the `if err == nil { ... }` block and records `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...)` (line 137), labeling this as a cache miss even though the cache was actually hit (just didn't contain the requested permission). This produces misleading cache-hit-ratio metrics for operators monitoring cache effectiveness.

findings.title: Denial-cache short-circuit test doesn't verify the cache path was actually used
findings.body: The subtest 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' sets s.permDenialCache and expects resp.Allowed == false, but it never asserts that the fallback store/identity lookups were skipped (e.g. via store.calls == 0). Since the default fakeStore used by setupService() returns no permissions anyway, the test would still pass with the same expected result even if the denial-cache short-circuit logic in Check() were removed entirely. This test therefore does not actually validate the new denial-cache behavior and would not catch a regression.

findings.title: Removing client-side cache for in-proc AuthZ client increases per-call overhead
findings.body: ProvideAuthZClient now wires the in-proc client with a NoopCache instead of a local cache, meaning every single Check/List call goes through the full inprocgrpc channel (including proto marshal/unmarshal through the gRPC interceptor chain) rather than being served from a short-lived client-side cache. For code paths that perform many individual Check calls in a loop (e.g., per-item authorization checks), this removes a previously-available fast path and could noticeably increase per-request latency/CPU, even though the server now has its own cache, because the gRPC call overhead itself is no longer avoided on repeated checks within the same request.
